utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Misetic, are you ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 56, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony; that is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Witness 56.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about a paragraph in your witness statement which has now been marked as P286. It is the witness statement from 1996. Do you have a copy of that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if the page numbering is going to the same. But in the English version, it is the bottom of page 7 and the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, from your questioning yesterday, we returned into open session when we adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I need to go into private session then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Rather have a break, perhaps, first. Let me just check one second. Yes. We will have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Before we continue I would like to request - and I apologies, I really do - that the documents D261, 62, and 63 should be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D261, D262, and D263 are admitted, under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Although I said that we could pass to the public session, I would like to remain on private session just for two more documents, and then we can continue on the public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registry please now show us Exhibit P190; this is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the map to appear on our monitor, in view of your service, I assume, but please correct me if I'm wrong, you were familiar with the area of the Drnis-Benkovac municipalities, that area of Dalmatia, the hinterlands of Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to assist us and the Trial Chamber regarding something that was unclear from previous hearings, the existence of two locales with the same name: The village of Gracac and the town of Gracac in Lika. My question is: Do you know where the village of Gracac is located, near Skradin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know where that village is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registry please zoom in on the lower middle section of the map, please. Lower central part, perhaps a little bit lower on the map. Near the town to of Skradin which is located a little bit to the ride of the Prokon lake which is marked in blue, so it's the lower left part of the map. So can you please zoom in on that section of map. Now this is in the middle in the lower middle section. A little bit more, please, and can you zoom in on that area a little bit more. This is wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can see in the middle of the map the town called Skradin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you go in the direction of north, north-west, if you follow the road there, do you see where the village of Gracac is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Chamber perhaps like the witness to mark the village in blue, and then we can have this admitted into evidence. I would suggest this be done in order for us to clarify that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand there's a town of Gracac and a village of Gracac. Why not agree on that it is there, find it on the map, and then why ask questions about it from witnesses. I mean, this is a matter which, I take it, is not contested, apart from which witness at any later stage refers to the town or to the village. That's, of course, another matter. But merely the location of a village and a town, it is a waste of time to bother a witness with that. Rather ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will follow your guidance. My only purpose was, although the witness is from that area, so that he could confirm that the geographical structure in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. If the parties agree that there's a town of Gracac and a village of Gracac, then, of course, the Chamber will always be aware that if someone talks about Gracac, that we have to clearly distinguish between whether it is town or village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your earlier testimony, you spoke about civil protection. I'll go through this subject very quickly. Can you confirm that the system of civil protection was positioned within the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's what the regulations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The commander was Mr. Milivoj Dondur. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Knin, it was Milivoj Dondur, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 2000, you mentioned that seven to ten days before Operation Storm began, in the northern barracks, there was a meeting to prepare the evacuation plan. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by Mr. Veso Kozomara, commander of the 7th Dalmatia Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that, at that time, well-informed civilians were leaving Knin. Can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, this situation arose primarily because of the advance of the Croatian army in the part of the front line leaning towards Grahovo, and the population of the town of Knin itself and the surrounding area closer to Grahovo, I mean primarily Strmica and Golubic, gradually began to pull out into safer areas because the population of Knin was originally from those surrounding villages. And if somebody had the opportunity to go to their native village, to go anywhere from this town that was expected to be attacked, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. So, from your statement, I see that on the 5th, there was a massive evacuation of the population, and you described these columns of people going towards Srb. Can you confirm that among the civilians in those convoys, there were also soldiers of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina with all their weaponry, tanks, Howitzers, cannons, rifles, and military vehicles. I'm referring to your statement from 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that perhaps somebody left behind some weapons, maybe a tank or another weapon, but there was military equipment in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Srb, which was an assembly point for the people, can you confirm that during those days, around 2.500 to 3.000 soldiers of the army of RSK gathered there and wanted to form a new line of defence in the canyon, in the gorge, as said in the book of Rade Cubrilo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that book, but I thought that he was not reliable enough to write such a book. He was not the right person to write something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification. In your statement of 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want, let's turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your statement of 2000, page 5, last paragraph, you mentioned Special Units of the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; page 5, last paragraph. And you also said, at the same time, that those units were the same as military troops, only in different uniforms, and that it was a consequence of the Vance-Owen Plan forbidding Republic of Serbian Krajina to have its own army. One clarification first. I suppose it was a mistake. You meant the Vance-Owen Plan [as interpreted], because the Vance-Owen Plan refers to Bosnia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Vance plan envisaged four UNPA zones, the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Croatia, the return of refugees, and demilitarisation. That was the gist of the Vance Plan, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, this circumstance, that the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in fact, existed and that Special Units of the police were part of that army, wasn't it a travesty of the plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, as I said, the Special Units of the police were actually the army troops, only dressed in different uniforms. Nothing else. Therefore, I would agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have two short topics remaining; cooperation with the civilian police of the United Nations, UNCIVPOL. Again, trying to avoid identifying answers, could you describe this cooperation? What was the procedure for contacts between your police force and the UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment the members of UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL arrived in May 1992, and all the way up to 1995, I can say that the cooperation between the police of Krajina and them was good. Sometimes we went on joint patrols in certain areas when it was in the interests of the local population, and we informed one another of certain matters relevant to the overall safety and security of people in that area. We would go to their offices, they would come to ours, we had joint meetings discussing all outstanding problems, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We understood that; however, what I'm really interested in is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness 56, since the Bench has no further questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this Court. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming a long way and answering all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again. Perhaps you'd stay for a few seconds, in view of the protective measures. We'll have a break. Then, I take it, that the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness. No protective measures for the next witnesses. Then I have one scheduling issue which I would just like to address very briefly. For the witness to come after the next witness, no protective measures either? That's the witness who is available only on Thursday, at least that's what --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, I will try to be as cautious as can be, because sometimes matters change. This is not an invitation, by the way. For the next witness with whom we'll start after the break, how much time would the Prosecution need? I think it was scheduled for one hour and a half, is that correct Mr. Russo, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness was originally scheduled for two and a half hours, but I think I can do it in two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can do it in two. How much time would the Defence need for the next witness to come, the next witness being Witness - let me just see - Mr. Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will be under half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, about two to three hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, half an hour to an hour, depending on what happens in front me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings altogether three and a half hours plus two hours, so that is five and a half hours. We have available tomorrow four hours. We will have able today another 55 minutes. Yes, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do my best to cut my examination shorter than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking this because the witness to come after the witness who we'll see later this morning, that's Witness 135, I'm informed that this witness is available only on Thursday. Now from what I understand, the Prosecution would need with that witness approximately one hour, if I'm well-informed. I also was informed that two of the three Defence teams would not cross-examine, at least at this moment for Witness 135, do not expect that they will have any questions in cross-examination. I see this is true from Markac and Cermak Defence. Mr. Kehoe, how much time do you think you will need. We are talking about Witness 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am familiar. Judge, I have been concentrating on this witness that is coming to the bar first, but I do believe that I can complete that in the Thursday time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber will not prepare for any additional time Thursday in the afternoon, expecting that the Prosecution will stick to its one hour and expecting that you'll have sufficient time until quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is on the record. I will be strict in this respect. No five minutes because it would mean to recall the witness once he has travelled back to where he comes from, and that would be for just a couple of minutes just a matter of discipline and efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you again, and sorry for bothering you with matters which are not relevant for you. We will have a break and resume at five minutes to 1.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, just a brief observation in relation to the previous witness. Mr. Mikulicic, that a statement which was put to the witness was marked for identification. We have had similar situations a couple of time the. We have had it in relation to Mr. Tchernetsky who was on the list of the Prosecution. At this stage, it was not a real problem there. We also had it in relation to some statements taken by the Defence which were put to Mr. Gojanovic; for example, D201 and 202. That is also where the village of Gracac in those statements appear, rather than in the testimony and Mr. Misetic had sought clarification on the issue village or town, already. Now the witness statement which was MFI'd this morning is of a witness who is not, or at least not anymore, on the list of witnesses for the Prosecution. So the Chamber will just wait and see whether this witness ever appears and whether this witness will ever attest. I can't say call him as a witness in the Defence case, because I don't know whether there will be a Defence case. So, therefore, the Chamber just waits and sees what will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, Mr. Russo, I take it, it will you who examines the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And the Prosecution will call John Geoffrey William Hill, Witness 123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, perhaps a very practical way of proceeding is not to ask attestations on each separate statement but perhaps put them all, ask whether this is the testimony, and then at the end ask him whether for all statements, because there is a quite a lot of them, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That was my intention, and there are also will be a few corrections which I'll lead him through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Hill. I take it that you can hear me in a language that you understand. Mr. Hill, before you give in evidence this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hill. Please be seated. You will first be examined, although from what I understand very much on the basis of statements already given, by Mr. Russo who is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, Will you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: John Geoffrey William Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you recall giving four statements to the ICTY: One dated 23 August 1996; the next, 28 to 29 May, 1997; the third on 1st November 1999; and the 4 fourth on 16 November 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions an answer for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, and I apologise to the interpreters. If I could have the assistance of the court usher, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to give the witness hard copies of his statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, did you have a chance to review all of your statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in the course after that review, did you find a number of corrections to be made to a few of those statements?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like you to take you through those corrections if I could. Let turn to your first statement page 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we get them in on the screen so that we can following the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be 65 ter 4913.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 65 ter numbers are usually not working, but for Mr. Registrar that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that would be, on the actual statement, page 0042-3175 by the ERN.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, looking towards the sort of middle of the page, the third section there, that paragraph that begins, "at the end of July," the second paragraph indicates: On the 31st of July, there was some shelling of Strmica where a Kenyan company HQ was located." Do you have a correction to the location where the Kenyan company HQ was located and where these events happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: That was in Vrlika, by Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hill, the Chamber always invites everyone to be as sufficient as possible. This has resulted in the speed of speech in which I don't know yet who is going to win, Mr. Russo or you. But the time I took is in order to give an opportunity for the interpreters to translate what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, if we could now move to your second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 4914, and this would be at the page 0057-7643. And if we could turn to 0057-7643, it would be at line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And at line 9, you indicate: "Then there was on a particular day, it was close to the 5th, probably the Monday or the Tuesday," where you give a discussion of shelling which occurred in Strmica. Was the Monday or Tuesday, was that intended to be before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the 5th then being actually the 4th of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could stay with that statement, move to page 7655, and beginning at line 20, where you indicate: "Then around supper time, I was sent. I took a couple of APCs, and I was going into town to get some patients at the hospital because apparently there were civilians at the hospital." Do you have a correction about the reason that you were actually going into town that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I don't recall the reason I was sent to go downtown at that day at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you don't recall it being to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could move now to page 7698, and beginning at line 19, where you discuss a town that you saw burning, and you call it Pecare, P-e-c-a-r-e, was that actually intended to refer to Pecane, P-e-c-a-n-e?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And there are a number of references to the name of that town going all the way to 7702, and all of those references are supposed to reference to Pecane. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And with regard to that same incident that is reported there, you make reference to the civilian police being the people that you saw in that town. Was that intended to refer to the civilian police or to a different type of police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: That's in reference to the Special Police, the dark blue uniforms with the armoured vehicles with the cannons that were dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, finally, moving to page 7721 and beginning at approximately line 5, where you are having a discussion regarding which units were in Operation Storm coming through Obrovac; and, again, you refer to the civilian police. Is that also intended to refer to the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. And those references continue on to the second page, 7722, at line 10, where it also indicates civilian police. The line says: "A total of six, one is civilian police." Was that also supposed to refer to the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Hill, with those corrections that we've just identified, as a whole, are the four statements that you made to the ICTY true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do those statements, given the corrections, accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were examined on those same matters here today in court, given your corrections, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I will tender the four exhibits. That would be 65 ter number 4913, which is the 23 August 1996 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, I encouraged Mr. Russo to take a bit of an abbreviated route to tendering. We have not gone through all the signatures and all the pages, et cetera. If there would be any challenge on what the witness just said relates to what we had on paper and which is uploaded into e-court, then I'd like to know it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, we have no objection. As a matter of fact, just to expedite matters, if Mr. Russo could just offer these four in, certainly it would move this along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that is the same for the other Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have, Mr. Russo, we have, in your 92 ter request or submission motion, we have two questions. The first is about the statements. We'll deal with those first. Witness statement dated 23 August 1996, Mr. Registrar that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've seen from the written submissions no objections, so P291 is admitted into evidence. The next one, Mr. Russo, I take it, is the witness statement dated 28th, 29th of May. 65 ter number 4914, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P229, no objections, therefore admitted into evidence. Third one is the 1st of November, 1999 statement, 65 ter 4915. No objections. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P293 is admitted into evidence. Last is witness statement dated the 16th of November, 2007. Also no objections from, as I take it, from the written submissions. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit P294, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Then there was another request; that is, to add 14 photographs to your 65 ter exhibit list. From the written submissions, I learned that none of the Defence teams object to it. Therefore, hereby the request to add the 14 photographs as specified in your request to the 65 ter list is granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time, I would like to read a 92 ter summary for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. Mr. Hill, you are aware that the reason for reading out a summary is that the public knows what we find in your statements. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Geoff Hill was the commander of the United Nations Military Police in Sector South from June until December 1995. Prior to Operation Storm, he liaised with the RSK minister of the interior and chief of police in Knin, and worked to maintain the security of UN personnel throughout Sector South, and to prevent hijacks and theft the UN equipment. He was present in Knin during the artillery attacks on 4 and 5 August 1995, and observed the shelling of Knin from the UNHCR compound. After Operation Storm, he managed to leave the UN HQ compound during the HV blockade and gain access to many areas in Sector South where he observed shelling damage and also witnessed HV soldiers, Special Police, and civilian police engaged in looting or acts of destruction. He also discovered several dead bodies and evidence of killings on the road used by the Serbs to flee the Krajina. Mr. Hill also gained the trust of a HV military police commander named Ivan Juric, who indicated that he was in charge of all military police units in the territory of the former RSK, including their anti-terrorist unit, and who provided Mr. Hill with information regarding the conduct of Operation Storm and the fact that all Serbs in the territory of the former RSK were considered terrorists. That concludes my summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, I'd like to begin with the situation in Knin immediately prior to Operation Storm. If you could refer, please, to your first statement, and that is P291 at page 3. And in the middle of that page, you indicate that you didn't see any heavy ARSK military equipment in Knin. Can you tell the Court what, if any, preparations you saw being made for a defence of Knin immediately prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see any extra activities that would be referring to a defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was there any organised removal of civilians prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did any local civilian employees not show up for work before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the shelling that happened on 4 August. If you could please explain to the Court what you personally observed or heard of the shelling on that day.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: On that morning at 0500 exactly, an artillery barrage started of Knin, in what I believe was from the south and the east. It was hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of artillery rounds. I immediately moved with the platoon I had on the grass to the back of the MP building, taking two MPs out of building and sending them up to their bunkers. We stayed in the bunker. It was for the escort platoon. There was two major salvos. I believe one was about 30 minutes, long followed by a pause which I had believed would be for them to reload to restock, and then another 30 minutes. It was hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of roads. I was in the bunker with the platoon this way to me. The doors were open approximately this wide, and I could see out over the town and there was orange glows and original bursts from the air-bursts of the artillery. That went on for approximately 90 minutes, and there was enough of a lull that I could then move up to the top of the camp where my MP platoon was to my bunker. My bunker is on the edge of the camp with the ARSK camp, and I'm looking directly into Knin. The shelling continued. It was getting to the point where we could listen to how close the round was coming in and observe. I took some photos of the town being shelled. At that point -- or during that time, a mortar round impacted the building directly over my head on the corner. A subsequent UNMO CBA or CDA was done to say that is was an 82-millimetre mortar from the ARSK. And a rifle propelled grenade passed the entrance the bunker and detonated approximately six feet off the ground back to my left, and blew myself and Corporal - I don't recall his name - down the stairs. We lost helmet, and we lost our weapons. And at that point, the shelling abated to the point where it was just harassment, rather than a massive salvo of hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Russo, the opening the witness indicated was approximately 20 to 25 centimetres, which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two doors I left open so that I could see out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're gestures do not appear on the transcript. That's the reason I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, you mentioned what you could see through the doors of this container, and that you could see air-bursts and I think you said glowing. If you could explain to the Court what air-burst is and how you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I was a reserve artillery officer before becoming a military police officer in the Canadian army. There is three types that you can use in artillery. When you want to attack and destroy a position on the ground, you use PD, point detonating. The round goes off when it hits. If it's reinforced, then you want the round go into the ground and then detonate. It is called delay. The third type is called air-burst. It is designed to go off, I believe - you can set it different heights - but approximately 20 metres above the ground. And it will spread the shrapnel over a very large area. It is designed to kill troops in the open. An example is the typical trench you might see in World War One is very deep. If an artillery rounds hits the ground beside the trench, the soldiers are safe. If it detonates above the trench and spreads the shrapnel out and they are unprotected, which they are, then it would cause an awful lot of injuries and death. This was occurring over Knin by me seeing the original glows from the bursts of the air-burst artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And continuing on that first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo and Mr. Hill, I don't know yet who is going to win, but you're both in a good position, and the interpreters and court reporters ask you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies to the interpreters. I will make an effort to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Hill, I think on the same page, and I think also during the summary you just gave us, you used the term "harassment fire" which you indicated was the kind of shelling that was occurring after the initial salvos. Can you please explain to the Court what you mean by harassment fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: It's a term, I believe, first used by the Americans in World War II, and then later in Vietnam. When you're shelling a position of force, they are putting artillery rounds into the area, not in massive salvos of hundreds and hundreds of rounds, but perhaps one, two, three, four rounds, a break, another round, another round. So it's enough that the enemy is aware they are being attacked. It limits movement, it limits resupply, and it basically is harassing the enemy rather than an all out offensive, like very earlier in the morning where there are hundreds and hundreds of rounds. So, in the morning, there was that initial attack, hundreds and hundreds and hundreds. It abated to this through the day; and then later in the evens prior to 2300, it picked up again to be the second highest level of shelling for the day in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter number 4899.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, do you recognise what's in that picture that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: That is my accommodation at the very top of our base. Overlooking, to the right of the photograph, this would a straight shot looking over Knin; and on the far corner below is where my bunker was for those two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If you were standing on the top of that bunker, what would your view be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: The town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P295 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could just get an indication of when the picture was taken. I don't know if that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not against admission but an additional question. Mr. Hill, could you tell us when this picture was taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately, during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It would have been during the month of July/August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prior to or after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell that you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could now have 65 ter 4900.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, looking at that photograph, I take it, was that taken on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Taken from my bunker, and I believe that's the POL compound area of Knin being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd move for the admission of 65 ter 4900.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any observations, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P296, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P296 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, moving now forward to the afternoon of the 4th of August, and staying on the same paragraph. I believe it is the third paragraph down, you indicate that you found a piece of a mortar shell inside the camp which you later showed to someone else. This is on your first statement, the third full paragraph towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Page 4. Can you please explain to the Court what it is that you found and what you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Walking back from the orders group of 1400 to my office, I found a very large piece of shrapnel. It was quite different than the shrapnel we had found before, which was from artillery. It was very thick and very big, perhaps three-eighths to half of an inch thick and five to six inches long, I didn't know what it was. I took it to Master Bombardier Parlee, who is a gunner, and asked what it was, and he said it was a casing to a 120-millimetre mortar round.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving to the next paragraph down on that same page, that's the final paragraph. You describe an incident or something that you witnessed in Knin which you called "counter-battery fire" occurring within your view. Can you please explain that incident to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: As the bombardment of the town abated to the point where it was what I would call harassment, I would watch them shell with my binoculars. On a ridge on, I believe, east of Knin, I saw what I believe to be puffs coming from HVR artillery on the lee side of the ridge. At that point, an impact of six to eight rounds came in a direct straight line, called the linear, on the ridge. From my artillery training, normally when you fire artillery, artillery will land in a group. But what you can do for a linear is you make it so that you fire the rounds in a straight, long line. It is designed that if you have, for example, a trench system the top of a hill, you can put the rounds into the trench system or a line of guns. So. I concluded there was a line of HV guns on the lee side, and the Serbs had struck with one to rounds per guns. So it was approximately six to eight rounds, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, along the ridge exactly in a line, and they did that three times. I was quite impressed by the capability of the guns to be able to hit that well in such a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter 5170.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: That's the area where I saw the counter-battery fire on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can I take that to mean that the area circled in red is where you saw that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would move for admission of 65 ter 5170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my orientation, could you tell us from what direction and from where this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This picture, I don't know, I did not take it. But it would have been -- the ridge was east from my view from my bunker on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, but, please correct me when I'm wrong, I see at least a railway complex, approximately on the right part of the photograph, just below the middle. It gives me the impression that this photograph was taken from approximately the area of the fortress or the castle, and then it would be approximately a north-easterly direction. Is that correct? I'm just thinking allowed so that I do not remain with a totally inadequate understanding of what this photograph presents us. I see no comments or no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are correct. The photo was taken from the castle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Number to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then P297 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, you mentioned earlier that sometime later in the evening, approximately around 2300 hours, the shelling picked up in intensity. I'd like to know, prior to that time, did you learn whether or not the shell would go continue on the following day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: At an orders group at 2100 hours in the headquarters, we were told that the HV would attack again at 0500 hours the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And by the time that you learned that, at 2100 hours, had the town of Knin been shelled for pretty much the entire day up to that point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And moving now to the time that you said the shelling picked up at about 2300 hours, can you tell the Court what you were doing at about 2300 hours?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I was summonsed to the front gate of the camp where I met the Chief of Staff, Colonel Leslie, at the time. General Forand, our commander, had decided that he would take in the Serb refugees. They had been accumulating at the gate throughout the day, seeking refuge from the shelling. At that point, there was in excess of 300. General Forand directed they would come in. The task was given to me. Colonel Leslie left. I used my escort platoon and my MP platoon, and we brought all the refugees in, searched them, lodged them in, I believe, one of the bars on base, as well as an auditorium and a gym; then began the process of searching, taking them to meals, putting a wire compound around which later eventually rose to over 850 and half our camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, starting at 2300 hours, how long it took you to process everyone in on that night?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Until approximately 0230 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Was there shelling continuing during this entire period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling had picked up. After I had given the tasks to all the individuals, I sent down on the steps of the headquarters building to have a cigarette. And I'd found another piece of shrapnel in the compound and I remember thinking with all of the shelling that was going on, we were in an open courtyard where my men were dealing with the refugees. I remember thinking that it was all it took was one artillery round in had a courtyard and most of my unit would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, can you give the Court an idea of what the makeup of what this group of refugees was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Women, children, old men, old ladies. There were some military-aged individuals in it. Basically, people that have come from the town. They had some bags, some personal belongs as they came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you find weapons on any of them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Found one AK, one Russian grenade, and several knives on individuals that we searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now If we can move to the following day, the 5th of August, and if you could tell the Court, again, what you personally observed or heard of the shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: At approximately 0510, the shelling started again, same as the 4th, in extremely large volumes, hundreds and hundreds of round, slightly less than the bombardment on the morning of the 4th, throughout the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in your first statement, at page 5, in the third full paragraph, you mention an incident where an artillery round impacted at the corner of the UN compound. Can you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I was at the main gate, seeing how the processing of refugees was happening. It was an ongoing process. As they came to the gate, they were admitted, they were searched, and interned. At approximately, an artillery round --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps resume there. Your answer started with: "I was at the main gate, seeing how the processing of refugees was happening. It was an ongoing process. As they came to the gate, they were admitted, they were searched," and then what did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Interned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, please, continue slowly with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was approximately 0930 hours. While talking to my commander, General Forand, an artillery round hit the wire at the corner of our camp. General Forand instructed me to go and check what had occurred. I left the camp with a number of soldiers. I got to the T-intersection, just outside the camp. I had also brought an OT-64 with me, and I saw six individuals who had been killed. Four were wounded, a mixture of civilian and military - I do not recall the exact mix - laying on the ground on that road from the intersection, a little up past the camp. I went back into the camp. I requested an engineer, a Canadian engineer, to go and clear the bodies of any potential booby traps. Then at that point, I was tasked by General Forand to set up a patrol within the camp, because the Jordanian troops were not going into their fighting positions. They were staying in their bunkers. My soldiers were to go around and get them in their firing positions. I later learned that the bodies were all bagged by the individuals that went out with me. All the weapons, grenade, rockets were taken offer the soldiers who were ARSK, and lodged in my cell area. And that's the last dealing I had with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 4912.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, can you describe this photograph for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: At the T-interpretation in front of our camp, one road leads to the right into Knin, and one out. This is a long building. This building was behind those soldiers when they were killed by the artillery round, and that is an example of how the shrapnel from that round had spread out over the street. So I took that picture to document it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have 65 ter 4912 admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P298 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, you indicated that the bodies at the intersection were bagged by some of the people that you had gone out with. Do you know what happened to those bodies later on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: They were bagged in the black body-bags that we had and put by the side of the road, across from the camp on a road leading upwards out of Knin. I was told that HV, when they were martialing to go into Knin for the last night, fired AKs into the bodies after opening the bags, and that urinated and defecated on the bodies. At a later date, the bodies were there for quite some time. I recall seeing them with the bags opened, and one body in particular had been -- had feces on the body and the bodies shot, even though the bodies died or the cause of death was the artillery round.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. At some point later in the day, in your statement, you indicate that the HV entered the town -- or, actually, that they had come to the UN compound. Can you describe for the Court how they came to the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: This is the first time that they came?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. When was the first time you saw them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: It was around noon that they came in, from around to the right of camp, where the Serb or ARSK barracks were. They arrived with three tanks, T-54, 55 -- I'm sorry, six tanks, T-54, 55, and three APCs, T-80s, with troops on foot. We talked to them. General Leslie -- they wanted to come into the camp and take the refugees, and I'm sorry, Colonel Leslie, at the time, was negotiating. He eventually negotiated that the Croats would stay out of the camp. The Croats told us that "We must stay in the camp." I was there discussing with the soldiers. Two of them were Canadians. One was on top of a tank. I talked to him and asked him how the offensive had gone. They said they took 30 hours to take Drnis, and then it only took five from there to Knin. I asked what they were going to do. He said they were going to kill all the Serb. The other individual, who was from, I believe, Montreal or Ottawa, was on the left, was infanteer. And I had asked him, because he spoke good English, what he was doing there, and he said he had come back to fight against the Serbs and that he had been waiting for this since 1945. He was approximately 22 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Hill, your -- do you know what unit of the HV they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: I believe this was the Pumas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Why do you believe that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: By their patches, they were known as the Puma Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And referring to your second statement this time, that would be P292, I believe, at page 0057-7655. That is, again, beginning at line 20, where you describe trying to get into the town of Knin. Can you tell the Court about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL
utterances.text: Around supper time, I took two OT-64 and two M-113 APCs to go into town, to try to get back any refugees that we could find. We went down the road to the T-intersection, where that building was I showed with the damage; turned right and got almost down to the gas station. There was one T-54 tank in front of us. They started to move the tank, but then a commander came, either a captain or a major HV. And he got extremely agitated, and I said we were going into town. We were UN, we were trying to find refugees. He absolutely refused, he said it was forbidden, he put tank across the road, he was quite angry, and he ordered us back to camp. When you looked behind, and turned around from the gas station and looked up the road, beside our camp, the entire road to the top of the hill was lined, front to back, of tanks and APCs of HV with infantry on top. And it was their assembly area before their final assault on Knin. After talking to this major, he had talked about taking our pistols, and he had later put a tank in front of the gate to come and take our pistols and then later removed. And we were told that we could not go into Knin that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will be moving to a new topic after this. I don't know if this is an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is. Mr. Hill, we will adjourn for the day. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether the testimony you already given or the testimony still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom. We stand adjourned until the 28th of May, 9.00, this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of May, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
